questions.q: In GitOps, what does it mean for Git to be the "single source of truth" for a cluster?
options: Git is just a backup location that is restored from only during a disaster
The live cluster state is expected to match what's committed to Git, and any divergence means the cluster, not Git, is wrong
Every developer keeps a personal fork that represents their own preferred cluster state
The cluster's etcd database is mirrored into Git automatically every night
questions.explain: The core GitOps claim is that Git holds the authoritative desired state; if the live cluster disagrees, the cluster is considered wrong and should be brought back in line with Git, not the other way around.

questions.q: Which command is declarative rather than imperative?
options: kubectl scale deployment payments-api --replicas=5
kubectl create deployment payments-api --image=registry/payments-api:1.4.2
kubectl edit deployment payments-api
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml, where deployment.yaml specifies replicas: 5
questions.explain: A declarative manifest describes the desired end state and can be applied idempotently; kubectl scale, create, and edit are imperative commands that issue a one-time instruction with no durable record of the intended end state.

questions.q: According to the OpenGitOps principles covered in this lesson, what does "Declarative" require?
options: That a system's desired state be expressed as a description of the end state, not as a sequence of imperative commands
That every deployment be written in Helm specifically rather than plain YAML
That the cluster reject any manifest that isn't signed by a certificate authority
That changes be applied by SSHing into cluster nodes directly
questions.explain: The OpenGitOps Declarative principle requires desired state to be expressed declaratively (what the end state should look like), as opposed to imperative scripts describing a sequence of actions.

questions.q: Why does a Git repository naturally satisfy the OpenGitOps "Versioned and Immutable" principle?
options: Because kubectl automatically writes every change back into a connected Git repository
Because Git commits are immutable, content-addressed snapshots, and the commit log preserves a complete version history that can be diffed or reverted
Because Git silently overwrites older commits to save storage space, keeping the repo small
Because Kubernetes refuses to apply any manifest that lacks a matching Git tag
questions.explain: Every Git commit is an immutable snapshot, and the commit history gives a complete, diffable, revertible record of every change — exactly what "Versioned and Immutable" calls for, with no extra tooling required.

questions.q: In the example repo layout from this lesson (apps/payments-api/base and apps/payments-api/overlays/<env>), what is the purpose of the overlays directories?
options: They hold a full, independent copy of every manifest for each environment, duplicated from scratch
They store the CI pipeline's build logs for each environment
They apply environment-specific patches (like replica counts or image tags) on top of the shared base manifest, typically via Kustomize
They contain the cluster's kubeconfig credentials for each environment
questions.explain: The base/ directory holds the common manifest; each overlays/<env>/ directory patches it with environment-specific differences, which is the standard Kustomize base-and-overlay pattern.
